tldr: The paper introduces EvoMAC, a self-evolving multi-agent collaboration network that iteratively adapts agents and their connections at test time using textual backpropagation, and proposes rSDE-Bench, a requirement-oriented software development benchmark with automatic evaluation.
contributions: EvoMAC: a novel self-evolving MAC network that iteratively adapts both agents and their connections during test time for each task
rSDE-Bench: the first benchmark featuring both complex/diverse software requirements and automatic evaluation of requirement correctness

Demonstration that automatic evaluation aligns with human evaluation at 99.22% coherence, and EvoMAC outperforms previous SOTAs by 26.48%, 34.78%, and 6.10% on Website Basic, Game Basic, and HumanEval respectively
methods: EvoMAC is inspired by neural network training and consists of three components: a coding team (MAC network) that generates code via feed-forward, a testing team that creates unit test cases as a target proxy, and an updating team that performs textual backpropagation to modify agent prompts and workflows based on compiler execution feedback. The process iteratively cycles through generation, verification, and update. rSDE-Bench contains 53 coding tasks with 616 requirements covering website and game software types at basic and advanced difficulty levels, each paired with black-box test cases for automatic evaluation.
results: Automatic evaluation in rSDE-Bench achieves 99.22% coherence with human evaluation. EvoMAC outperforms previous SOTA methods by 26.48% on Website Basic, 34.78% on Game Basic, and 6.10% on HumanEval. EvoMAC shows consistent improvement with more evolving iterations and performs well across different driving LLMs.
limitations: Current MAC systems rely on heuristic human-designed static systems with performance confined to human initialization and lack flexibility to adapt to new tasks. Self-critique strategies have limitations of subjective/biased critique and hallucination risks. Existing benchmarks are confined to function-level tasks or depend on expensive human evaluations, leaving a gap in comprehensive software-level assessment.
